content: A nasal voice refers to a specific type of speaking voice that is characterized by a distinct nasal quality. This quality can occur naturally due to genetic differences. In the context of vocal characteristics, the term nasal is the opposite of adenoidal or denasal. Nasal speech can be further categorized into two types: hypo-nasal speech and hyper-nasal speech. Hypo-nasal speech occurs when there is an insufficient amount of nasal airflow during speech. This results in a voice that sounds as though the individual has a severe cold. The causes of hypo-nasal speech are typically related to conditions that obstruct the nasal passages. These causes include, but are not limited to: Enlargement of the adenoids (adenoid hypertrophy) Enlargement of the nasal turbinates (turbinate hypertrophy) Allergic reactions affecting the nasal passages Sinus infections Viral upper respiratory infections A deviated nasal septum Hyper-nasal speech, on the other hand, is characterized by an excessive amount of nasal airflow during speech. This is particularly noticeable during the pronunciation of plosive and fricative sounds, which are syllables that begin with consonants. Common examples of conditions associated with hyper-nasal speech include cleft palate and velopharyngeal insufficiency, where the soft palate fails to close properly against the back of the throat during speech. Certain individuals are often described as having nasal voices. Examples include Fran Drescher, Ray Romano, Neil Young, Bob Dylan, John Lennon, Billy Corgan, and the character Janice from the sitcom Friends. Additionally, characters such as Clyde Donovan and Kyle Schwartz from the animated show South Park are also noted for their nasal vocal qualities.
